hypotheses.claim: The removal of index idx_tenant_status_name caused the search queries to fall back to full sequential scans, which saturated disk I/O and produced the observed latency spikes.
hypotheses.supporting_reasoning: Code evidence shows the index was deliberately dropped (EV-CODE-001, EV-CODE-003). The warning log (EV-LOG-004) records a query plan change to a sequential scan. Metrics confirm a surge in sequential scans (EV-MET-006) and strong correlations between sequential scans, disk read rate (EV-MET-007) and latency (EV-MET-008), matching the timing of I/O saturation (EV-LOG-001) and latency spikes (EV-LOG-002).
falsification_criteria: A post‑mortem schema inspection reveals that idx_tenant_status_name still exists after the deployment
Sequential scan count does not increase during the incident window
verification_plan: Inspect the database schema for the presence of idx_tenant_status_name
Run EXPLAIN on a representative search query to verify the execution plan uses a sequential scan
Correlate the timestamped sequential scan metric (EV-MET-006) with the I/O saturation log (EV-LOG-001)
Confirm that the index removal commit (EV-CODE-001) was applied to the production database

hypotheses.claim: An unexpected surge in overall CPU usage triggered the query optimizer to choose less efficient sequential scans, leading to disk I/O saturation and latency degradation.
hypotheses.supporting_reasoning: Metrics show CPU usage spiked to 99.5% (EV-MET-003) and exceeded the 90% threshold (EV-MET-004), with a 57.6‑point increase over baseline (EV-MET-005). High CPU can pressure the optimizer to favor cheaper planning paths, potentially resulting in sequential scans that overload the storage subsystem, as reflected by the I/O saturation log (EV-LOG-001) and latency spike (EV-LOG-002).
falsification_criteria: CPU usage remains below 80% throughout the incident period
No change in optimizer behavior is observed when CPU load is artificially increased
verification_plan: Review CPU utilization traces for the exact time window of the incident
Examine optimizer configuration and logs to see if high CPU triggered plan changes
Re‑run the same query under controlled CPU load to observe plan selection
Check whether the sequential scan metric (EV-MET-006) rises only when CPU spikes

hypotheses.claim: The yellow health status of the Elasticsearch cluster reduced query routing efficiency, contributing to increased latency independent of the database index removal.
hypotheses.supporting_reasoning: A warning log indicates the ES cluster entered YELLOW state with an unassigned replica shard (EV-LOG-003), which can degrade redundancy and routing. Concurrently, the application reported a latency spike (EV-LOG-002) and metrics record a latency increase to 3500 ms (EV-MET-001). This suggests the search service latency may be partially driven by ES cluster health rather than solely by DB I/O issues.
falsification_criteria: Elasticsearch cluster health remains GREEN during the latency spike
Latency returns to baseline while the cluster stays in YELLOW
verification_plan: Query the Elasticsearch cluster health API for the incident timeframe
Correlate cluster health changes with application latency metrics
Perform a controlled test by forcing a replica to be unassigned and measuring latency impact
Check whether database I/O metrics (disk read rate) remain stable while ES health degrades

proposals.rationale: The confirmed root cause is the removal of the idx_tenant_status_name index, causing queries to fall back to sequential scans and saturating I/O. Adding the index back in the MockDatabase initialization ensures the search logic detects the index and avoids table scans, directly addressing the performance degradation.

changes.description: Initialize MockDatabase with the required compound index so that search_items uses the index path instead of performing a full table scan.

proposals.rationale: The confirmed hypothesis shows that the ES cluster being YELLOW degraded query routing efficiency, causing latency spikes. By checking cluster health and short‑circuiting searches when the cluster is not GREEN, the service avoids routing through an unhealthy cluster, mitigating the latency impact.
